title: Study Abroad Report: Medical University of Vienna
paragraphs: This year I studied abroad at the Medical University of Vienna in Austria. I was able to do a fulfilling total of 11 weeks of clerkship: 4 weeks of thoracic surgery, 4 weeks of family medicine and 3 weeks of emergency medicine. Below I summarize the content of the clerkships and what I felt as my report.

[Thoracic surgery] The reason I chose thoracic surgery as a clerkship was a very vague one: a student from Vienna who had come on exchange the previous year told me it is famous for actively performing lung transplants worldwide (over 200 cases a year). My goal was to experience surgery that one can hardly see in Japan. First, a big difference from Japan regarding transplantation is how the intention to donate organs is expressed. In Japan, one can become a donor by carrying a donor card and indicating the intention to donate organs, but in Austria it is the opposite: a person who has been determined to be brain dead can become a donor unless they have indicated their intention by carrying a card refusing organ donation. For that reason the number of organ donations after brain death is large and many transplants can be performed. In addition, the university hospital has a transplant internal medicine department that manages the whole body after transplantation, and I felt that the existence of this too is an environment that makes it possible to actively perform transplants. The clerkship started with a conference at 7:30. Since there were exchange students and doctors from other countries who came to study transplantation, it was basically held in English. However, when the discussion got heated and someone started speaking in German, it switched to German from there, which was hard. After that, the students' work was to perform admission tests for newly admitted patients: blood draws, electrocardiograms, pulmonary function tests and so on. At first I could not draw blood well and was depressed at the gap with the local students, but I improved as I practiced.

[Family medicine] This is a program made for exchange students, and together with Mr. 畑下 and two older women doctors from Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan, we four visited and received explanations about medical facilities in the city of Vienna. The main places were a school doctor, an HIV facility, a long-term care hospital, a homeless shelter and so on. Here the pattern was mostly to receive an explanation in English and then have a discussion, and it was a valuable opportunity for thinking about the differences in medicine between Japan and other countries. I was also allowed to do a clerkship staying overnight at the home of a family doctor who had looked after the seniors who had studied in Vienna in past years. It was a very warm household, and although it was a three-night, four-day clerkship, they treated me like a real family, and when we parted I was truly sad.

[Emergency medicine] Here I did my clerkship mainly observing the initial response to walk-in patients while assisting in treatment. Since an intravenous line is placed in almost every patient, I did that job diligently and actively, and my skill in placing lines improved considerably. Overall, because patients understood the education of students, I could actively perform procedures and so on, and I was also allowed to observe night and weekend emergency care, and I was surprised at the high awareness of the local students who came to do the clerkship and observation. When I spoke to the doctors in their free time, they gave me simple lectures on things like diagnostic imaging and the use of ultrasound.
